introduction: These hundred readings describe one bounty received in different measures. The spirit, they say, shines on everything that exists: as cohesion in the mineral, growth in the plant, sense in the animal, reason in the human being, and beyond these the spirit of faith and the Holy Spirit. Each kingdom lives in its own degree and cannot comprehend the one above it. Beside them stand the old pictures of a ranked and living creation, from Genesis and the Psalms to Plotinus, Dante, Pope's chain of being and Rumi's ascent through the kingdoms. Other voices question the ranking or the boundaries: Darwin on degree and kind, the Preacher on one breath for man and beast, Bentham on suffering, Whitman among the animals, Heraclitus and Tennyson on strife in nature, Lucretius on a mind that dissolves, and the Gita on a spirit that returns.
questions: The readings compare God's grace to rain that takes the form of whatever receives it. Where have you seen one gift become different things in different people?
Darwin held that the human mind differs from the animal in degree, not kind; the readings name the rational soul as a distinct degree. What would settle the question for you?
Bentham asks whether a creature can suffer. What does a ranking of the kingdoms imply, and not imply, about how the lower ones should be treated?
One reading calls love the cause of all existence; Heraclitus and Tennyson see strife. How do you read the natural world?
The readings say a lower degree cannot comprehend a higher. What follows for how confidently human beings should speak about what is above them?
The readings hold that the spirit does not return to this world, against the Gita and Plato. What do you find persuasive on either side?

outside.why: Jesus said that the Father maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
Dante begins his Paradise: the glory of Him who moveth everything doth penetrate the universe, and shine in one part more and in another less.
Walt Whitman believed that a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.
Plotinus says that the One, seeking nothing and lacking nothing, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.
Paul told the Athenians that God needs nothing from human hands, seeing He giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.
Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things, all objects of all thought, and rolls through all things.
Paul prays for the whole spirit and soul and body of his friends, naming the three together.
Alexander Pope wrote of a vast chain of being, which from God began: natures ethereal, human, angel, man, beast, bird, fish, insect.
Darwin concluded that the difference in mind between man and the higher animals, great as it is, is one of degree and not of kind. Are the kinds of spirit steps on one slope, or distinct in kind?
Milton's angel tells Adam that all things proceed from one Almighty and up to Him return, each in its active sphere.
Paul says that all flesh is not the same flesh: there is one kind of men, another of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
Genesis says that God breathed into man's nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul.
The Preacher says that the dust shall return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
The same Preacher says that man hath no preeminence above a beast, for they have all one breath. What grounds are there for distinguishing a human spirit from the life shared with animals?
In Genesis God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree after his kind.
Then God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind.
The psalm says of all living things: Thou takest away their breath, they die; Thou sendest forth Thy spirit, they are created.
Jesus said that if his disciples should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
The Qur’an says that there is not a thing but hymneth His praise, but ye understand not their praise.
Job says: ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; in God's hand is the soul of every living thing.
Jeremy Bentham wrote of animals: the question is not, can they reason, nor can they talk, but can they suffer? What does a creature's degree of spirit have to do with how it should be treated?
Coleridge wrote of the one Life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul.
Shelley wrote that nothing in the world is single; all things by a law divine in one spirit meet and mingle.
The psalmist exclaims: O Lord, how manifold are Thy works; in wisdom hast Thou made them all.
The Qur’an says that there is not an animal in the earth, nor a creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you. What do the kingdoms share that a classification into ranks can hide?
Elihu says that there is a spirit in man, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
Marcus Aurelius asks his reader to regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul.
The psalmist says that man has been made a little lower than the angels and given dominion over the works of God's hands.
Hamlet calls man the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals.
Walt Whitman thought he could turn and live with animals, they are so placid and self-contained. Is being the highest of creatures the same as being the best of them?
Aristotle said that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice he is the worst of all. What does a higher degree of spirit make possible in both directions?
Leibniz held that each simple substance has relations which express all the others, and is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Aristotle begins his Metaphysics with the words: all men by nature desire to know.
Pope placed man on an isthmus of a middle state, in doubt to deem himself a god or beast. Is being the result of all the kingdoms a strength or a strain?
Pope wrote that from nature's chain whatever link you strike, tenth or ten thousandth, breaks the chain alike.
Proverbs names four things little upon the earth but exceeding wise: the ants, the conies, the locusts and the spider.
In the parable a man gave five talents to one servant, two to another and one to another, to every man according to his several ability.
Paul says that the body is one and hath many members, and all the members, being many, are one body.
This is the saying the question quotes: many are called, but few are chosen.
Paul writes that God hath mercy on whom He will, and asks who art thou that repliest against God. Is a difference of capacity a choosing, and if so, is it just?
The Qur’an says of the messengers themselves that some have been caused to excel others.
Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
The first letter of John says that love is of God, and that God is love.
Boethius wrote in prison that all things are seen to yearn in due time for due return.
Heraclitus said that war is the father of all and the king of all. Is it attraction or strife that holds the world together and moves it?

Tennyson wrote of one who trusted that love was creation's final law, though Nature, red in tooth and claw, shrieked against his creed. How is love as the cause of all existence squared with what animals do to one another?
The Letter to the Colossians says of the creating Word: by him all things consist.
Proverbs says that it is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Darwin looked at an entangled bank of plants, birds, insects and worms and saw forms produced by laws acting around us. How do a law of nature and a degree of spirit describe the same thing?
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the Son as upholding all things by the word of his power.
The psalm calls on fire and hail, snow and vapours, mountains and all hills to praise the Lord.
James says that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights.
In the parable the same seed falls by the way side, on stony places, among thorns and on good ground. Is the receptive degree of a thing fixed, or can ground be made ready?
Paul says that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.
Isaiah says that the mountains and the hills shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
Jesus said: consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin.
Wordsworth wrote that one impulse from a vernal wood may teach you more of man than all the sages can.
Thoreau asked: shall I not have intelligence with the earth? Am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself? What kinship with the lower kingdoms does a human being keep?
Rumi wrote: I died as inanimate matter and arose a plant, I died as a plant and rose again an animal, I died as an animal and arose a man.
Emerson wrote that, striving to be man, the worm mounts through all the spires of form.
Hamlet traces the dust of a conqueror: imperious Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might stop a hole to keep the wind away.
Plato observed that water by condensation becomes stone and earth, and the elements pass into one another.
Genesis says to the first man: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Whitman wrote: I bequeath myself to the dirt to grow from the grass I love; look for me under your boot-soles.
Heraclitus said that the way up and the way down is one and the same.
Darwin saw endless forms most beautiful evolved from a few forms or one. If each kingdom progresses within its own degree, how do you understand the passage from one kind of life to another?

The Bhagavad Gita says that as one lays aside worn-out robes and takes new ones, so the spirit puts by its garb of flesh and passes to another. What turns on the claim that the spirit does not return to this world?
Plato's Socrates reports the teaching that the soul has been born again many times and has seen all things. Why have so many held this view, and what is said against it here?
Paul says that what is sown is not the body that shall be, but bare grain, and God giveth it a body.
The psalmist considers the heavens and asks: what is man, that Thou art mindful of him?
Genesis says: thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.
The Qur’an describes stages: a drop, a clot, a little lump, bones, flesh, and then another creation.
Paul says that there is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, and one star differeth from another star in glory.
In Isaiah God says: as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my thoughts than your thoughts.
Paul says that the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit, neither can he know them.
Hamlet says that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in his friend's philosophy.
Jesus told his disciples on the night before he died: in my Father's house are many mansions.
The Preacher asks: who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward? What kind of knowledge is available about where a spirit goes?
Isaiah says that the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance.
Isaiah hears a voice: all flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field.
Mencius said that that whereby man differs from the lower animals is but small; the mass of people cast it away.
The psalm says: be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding.
Plato held that the capacity of learning exists in the soul already, and must be turned toward the light.
Proverbs describes a field left untended: it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof.
Jesus said: I am the vine, ye are the branches; without me ye can do nothing.
Paul says that we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office.
Locke supposed the mind at birth to be white paper, void of all characters, furnished by experience. Do people differ in innate capacity, or only in what has been written on them?
The Tao Te Ching says that the great Tao is all-pervading; all things depend on it for their production, which it gives to them.
The Rig Veda says: to what is One, sages give many a title.
The Chandogya Upanishad says that by one clod of clay all that is made of clay is known; the difference is only a name.
The Qur’an says that man was created from a product of wet earth, and then by stages produced as another creation.
Jesus said that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.

Lucretius held that the mind, like the body, is a compound that dissolves, so that death is nothing to us. If the lower spirits are powers that arise from combination, why is the human spirit not one more of them?
William Blake wrote of seeing a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower.
Hopkins wrote that the world is charged with the grandeur of God.
Pascal said that by space the universe swallows him up like an atom, and that his dignity lies in thought.
Plotinus likens what proceeds from the Supreme to the brilliant light encircling the sun, ceaselessly generated from that unchanging substance.
Cyprian wrote that there are many rays of the sun, but one light.
The Light Verse of the Qur’an speaks of a lamp in a glass, the glass as it were a shining star: light upon light.

romans-whole-creation-groaneth.text: For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope, Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now

corinthians-all-flesh-not-the-same.text: All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds. There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory

genesis-let-the-earth-bring-forth-grass.text: And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so. And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good

matthew-fowls-of-the-air.text: Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they

proverbs-conies.text: There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks; The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands; The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces

acts-life-and-breath-and-all-things.text: Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things
